prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping, and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for the optical lattice clock to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. What I check first in any measurement result is whether the number survives a different laboratory, and here it does. Several groups with different atoms, lasers, lattices and vacuum systems (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL and others) have compared lattice clocks at the 1e-18 level, and the same clocks resolve gravitational redshift across millimetres. The new idea is specific and physical. Magic-wavelength trapping lets thousands of atoms be held without Doppler, recoil or light-shift penalties, so the signal-to-noise gain of an ensemble no longer costs accuracy. That is not the frequency comb (a ruler for counting optical cycles) and not the single trapped ion; it is a different way to build the reference oscillator. In reply to the chair's request to test the case with the AMO members, I find nothing in the round-1 files that disputes the physics. The open questions are credit and wording. The convergence of seven members is partly mutual influence, as the chair says, and Lindroth and I should not be counted as two independent first choices. What I weigh is that no one has found a scientific flaw, and that the two members least comfortable (Olsson on Ye's role, Mehlig on discovery type) object on grounds the record can answer.
statement.case_against: The real weakness is not the clock but the allocation inside it. Katori proposed magic-wavelength lattice trapping and, with Takamoto, made the first Sr lattice clock demonstration. Ye's decisive contributions are different in kind: the JILA Sr lattice clock and its systematics, the long optical coherence times, the 1e-18 accuracy and stability, and the many-body, Fermi-degenerate operation. If the committee holds strictly that the prize is for the original invention, a Katori-centred citation can be argued, and Takamoto, Lemonde and SYRTE, Ludlow, the Yb and Hg lattice groups and the Al+ ion-clock line all have claims that three names cannot hold. The overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 1989 and 2012 prizes is also real and means the citation must say what is new. Finally, the fundamental-physics payoff (drifts of constants, dark matter) is still mostly prospective, and a thorium nuclear clock may later create a further claim by Ye.

responses.point: Olsson asks what in the record shows that Ye's contribution is original and decisive in its own right, not an improvement of Katori's invention to record accuracy; the chair put this to Johansson, Lindroth and me.
responses.response: I would put it concretely, from memory and not from verified sources. Katori's 2003 proposal and the 2005 Tokyo demonstration established that a magic-wavelength lattice could confine Sr atoms for spectroscopy. What turned this into a clock at the 1e-18 level was a long series of experimental steps in Ye's laboratory: second-scale optical coherence on the 1S0-3P0 line, the first systematic evaluation of the JILA Sr lattice clock, and the later work that controlled blackbody, density and lattice shifts, followed by the three-dimensional Fermi-degenerate lattice where performance is limited by atomic physics and not by technical noise. These are not refinements of a number. Each required identifying and measuring an effect that had not been controlled before, and each changed what other groups could do. Ye's earlier work with Kimble and Katori on state-insensitive trapping also shows he contributed to the underlying idea, though I would not base the citation on that. I accept that Ludlow, Bloom, Campbell, Marti and others did much of the hands-on work. That is normal under a three-person limit and does not make Ye's role derivative, but I agree the citation should say invention and realisation, so that it implies neither that Katori only had an idea nor that Ye only improved it.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B024 for its clean prediction-then-observation pattern and concedes that B052 is the safest configuration, arguing that the open pairing mechanism does not weaken the discovery of flat-band correlated phases.
responses.response: I accept the distinction between an unsettled interpretation and an unsettled discovery, and I am outside my competence on how robust the flat-band phenomenology is. I also grant that a measurement technique is not automatically lower than a new phase of matter, and that I may have weighted measurement too lightly against new phenomena in my own reasoning. My remaining reason for placing B024 behind B052 is not that it is less important. The allocation of the trio is still open (Cao as first author, the earlier Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto theory, the Dean, Young, Yazdani and Kim experiments), and the experiments are eight years old. I do not think B024 is at risk of being wrong, but I would rather see how the field sorts its credit before choosing three names. I keep it out of my alternatives for that reason, and I would not regard the committee as making a mistake if you continue to rank it first.

responses.point: The chair moved from IceCube first to B052, notes that atomic physics is outside his expertise, and asks the AMO members to test the B052 case; the summary also asks whether a two-part prize is possible and how the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers should be handled on B043.
responses.response: I tried to test it as an experimentalist in the field would, by asking whether the central numbers are what a skeptic would check and not what a proponent would quote. The 1e-18 systematic uncertainty is dominated by blackbody radiation and lattice light shifts, and comparison of clocks from different laboratories over fibre links is the strongest independent check available. On that basis I would say the maturity is in order. For B043, I still keep it as an alternative because a new observational window opened by an instrument is the kind of door I look for, but I agree with you that the source associations are at moderate significance and that credit for the earlier pioneers is harder to settle with two names. I would not make it a second part this year. That would put a mature result beside one whose main physics results are still being written, and the Halzen and Spiering allocation would need the pioneers addressed.

responses.point: Lindroth agrees on B052, wants the citation worded around the lattice clock and not the comb, keeps B035 as an alternative because of the Chu attribution problem, and asks that the committee be clear about which parts of the JILA record are Ye's own.
responses.response: I agree on both points and I have sharpened my wording since round 1 to name magic-wavelength trapping and the lattice clock explicitly. That answers the comb overlap and avoids pre-empting recognition of a thorium nuclear clock, which would be a different physical system. On B035 I now hold more firmly that it should not be a second part this year. A part with Pritchard, Bordé and Kasevich leaves Chu and the early demonstrations in a place I cannot defend, and a part with one person would be arbitrary, as you said. I still regard it as the natural future companion, since it and the lattice clock both extend quantum control to measurements of gravity and fundamental constants.

responses.point: Johansson, who ranked circuit QED first at opening, has withdrawn B056 over timing relative to the 2025 prize and the omission of Blais under the three-person cap, and treats the redefinition of the second as not a scientific criterion.
responses.response: I agree that the redefinition of the second is not a scientific criterion and I would not delay for it; it is a consequence that will follow from the physics, not a test of it. I also appreciate that you withdrew B056 yourself, because it simplifies my own conflict note: I am on the executive management of WACQT, which overlaps institutionally with your centre, and B056 and B044 are close to my field. Neither is now in any configuration, so I do not see a need for recusal on B052 and will raise it again only if one of them returns.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that Katori's and Ye's roles (concept and first demonstration; accuracy, coherence and many-body operation) are both original and decisive, or prefers a Katori-centred or differently composed credit. I am recalling priority details from memory and have not verified every date.
Whether the citation should name both 'invention' and 'realisation' as I propose, or be framed around accuracy, and whether such wording is enough to separate the prize from the 2005 comb prize.
How the claims of Takamoto, Lemonde and SYRTE, Ludlow and the Yb, Hg and Al+ clock groups should be weighed; three names cannot cover them.
Whether a later thorium nuclear clock or the SI redefinition should affect timing. I think not, but others may see it differently.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with Katori, Ye or the lattice-clock community; I have no collaboration with either. I am on the executive management of WACQT (Chalmers-led, institutionally overlapping with Johansson's centre) and in the management team of Deep Light Vision AB, an ultrasound optical tomography spin-off that uses spectral-hole-burning filters, which is unrelated to the lattice-clock work. WACQT relates to B056 and B044, neither of which is in any configuration now. My earlier work on rare-earth quantum memories and atomic spectroscopy is not connected to B052. I would raise recusal if B056 or B044 became live, but do not consider one necessary for B052.
